questions.q: Why is prompt injection possible in AI automations?
options: Models read instructions and data through the same channel: text
Attackers can edit a workflow's prompt once they know the platform
Models only follow instructions that arrive in a structured format
Automations encrypt prompts, which hides injected text from checks
questions.explain: Because instructions and data both arrive as text, text written by someone else, such as an email or web page, can try to act like instructions.

questions.q: An agent reads incoming customer emails, can look up private order history and can send email to any address. What does the lesson recommend?
options: Rely on labeling the emails as untrusted, which removes the risk
Break the combination, or put a human approval before anything leaves
Give the agent admin rights so it can verify each sender's identity
Add a stronger warning to the brief telling it to ignore instructions
questions.explain: This is the dangerous combination of private data, untrusted content and the ability to send information out, so the lesson says to remove a capability or require human approval before anything leaves.

questions.q: A teammate wants to paste your AI provider's API key into a shared spreadsheet so everyone can reuse it. What's the safer practice?
options: Share it, but rename the spreadsheet so outsiders can't find it
Use one key for every automation so there's only one to protect
Keep keys in a credential store, one per automation, with spending limits
Paste the key into each prompt instead, where only the AI can see it
questions.explain: The lesson says never to put keys in prompts, spreadsheets or documents; store them in a credential store or environment variables, one per automation, with spending limits and rotation.
